author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: One Door Closed by Choice
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
The door to my old room was still there.

I had avoided it for three days after the Lantern Walk, which was an impressive achievement considering it stood only a few turns from the square. It was an ordinary painted door set into a stretch of old stone. The Threadway did not advertise where it led. Only the small brass plate with my chosen name marked it as mine.

Maui stopped beside me.

"Do you want me to come?"

"Not yet."

He nodded.

I reached for the handle.

The brass was cold. When I turned it, a familiar smell met me: laundry soap, paper, and the faint dust of a room that had not been lived in for a while. The desk was where I remembered it. A book lay facedown beside a cup. The light came through the window at an angle I recognized without knowing why.

Then I noticed the notebook.

It sat beneath the lamp, bound in faded green cloth, with a ribbon I could have tied myself. I knew the handwriting on the first page before I read the words.

I had written a list of things I was afraid to ask for.

The first was simple: a day when I didn't have to explain myself.

The second had been crossed out so hard that the paper was nearly torn.

The third said: Don't let people decide where I belong just because they remember more than I do.

I sat on the edge of the bed.

I had expected the room to give me answers. Instead it gave me evidence of a person who had been frightened long before Lanternweald.

Footsteps sounded in the hall behind me.

Maui did not come through the door.

"Jasper?" he called.

"I'm here."

"Are you all right?"

I looked at the notebook.

"I don't know."

There was a long pause.

"Do you want me to wait?"

"Yes. Outside."

"All right."

I heard him move away from the doorway. Not far, but far enough to give me space.

That was harder than rescue. I knew it was harder for him, because it was hard for me too.

I stayed in the room for another twenty minutes. I opened the desk drawer and found a broken pen, two bus tickets, and a photograph turned facedown. I did not turn it over. I wasn't ready to look at a face I might not recognize.

Instead I wrote the date in the notebook.

I live somewhere else now.

The words looked absurdly small.

I added: That does not mean this room has stopped being mine.

When I finally stepped into the hall, Maui was sitting on the floor with his back against the wall. He had taken the opportunity to carve a tiny fish into the handle of his walking stick.

"You waited," I said.

"You asked."

"I thought you'd get bored."

"I did."

He held up the fish.

"I gave boredom a face."

It was a much better fish than the one on the broom handle.

I laughed.

Then I cried.

The tears surprised both of us. Maui stood, but he didn't reach for me until I stepped into his arms. His coat smelled of sea air and the smoke from Mara's bakery. I pressed my face against his shoulder and let the feelings come without arranging them into a story.

After a while he asked, "Do you want to go back in?"

"No."

"Do you want to close the door?"

"Yes."

I turned, took the handle, and pulled it shut.

The latch clicked. Nothing in the arch dimmed. No bell sounded in protest. The Threadway did not punish me for leaving a room I wasn't ready to inhabit.

I stood there for a moment, breathing.

"Is this running away?" I asked.

Maui considered the door.

"I don't think so."

"Why?"

"Because you know where it is. And you're deciding when to return."

I looked at him.

"That was a surprisingly good answer."

He grinned faintly.

"I'll try not to make a habit of it."

We walked back toward Tideglass in silence. Lanternwell Square smelled of bread and damp leaves. The frost was melting from the roofs. I noticed that the lantern I'd painted was still hanging beside the signal post, its wick extinguished and the circle of amber paint intact.

Before we reached home, I turned back toward the lantern by the signal post. The glass was misted from the cold. Somebody had replaced the wick while I was away, and the flame inside was steadier than the one I'd left.

"Who fixed it?" I asked.

"Mara mentioned a volunteer on the morning shift," Maui said. "They wrote it in the little service book."

I found the book beneath the sheltered ledge. My earlier repair was still recorded there, along with the name of the person who had checked it today. The place didn't stop working when I stepped through a door.

"That's a strange thing to be relieved about," I said.

"Is it?"

"I suppose I thought everybody would be waiting for me to tell them what happened."

Maui looked genuinely puzzled. "We wanted you safe. That's not the same as wanting a report."

The words struck harder than I expected. I had a green notebook filled with memories of being useful, and somewhere in it a list I'd been afraid to show anyone. I didn't want those old obligations to walk out of the room with me and start issuing new orders.

At the house, I set my boots by the stove and looked at the fish carving Maui had left there. Its tail was uneven. He'd spent the afternoon sanding it rather than trying to follow me through the doorway.

"Can we have dinner before we talk?" I asked.

"Yes."

"And if I only tell you half of it?"

"Then I'll know half."

"You're becoming dangerously sensible."

He grinned. "Don't tell anyone."

He set out bread and warmed soup while I changed into dry clothes. Nothing about the food was magnificent, but I found myself hungry for the first time all day. When I returned, he had pulled out the chair I liked without making a ceremony of it.

I took his hand briefly before we ate.

I didn't owe him every word in the green notebook to be worthy of his company. I could choose what to share and still choose to stay.

At home, I put the green notebook on the kitchen table.

Maui set down the fish carving beside it.

"Do you want to tell me what you found?" he asked.

"Some of it."

"Which part?"

"A list I wrote before I came here. Things I was afraid to ask for."

He sat opposite me.

"What did you ask for?"

"Mostly nothing."

He winced.

"That's not very you."

"It was me. Maybe it still is, sometimes."

He thought about that.

"I've been trying to learn how to ask instead of deciding for people," he said. "Maybe you're learning the same thing from the other side."

I looked at the notebook.

"Maybe."

I turned the page and wrote a new list. Not demands. Wishes.

I want to visit the old room again when I choose.

I want Maui to stay tonight.

I want room for other people I love without making anyone a substitute.

I want to know what the bell means, but not at the cost of my right to say no.

I read the list aloud.

Maui listened.

When I finished, he said, "I can say yes to one of those right now."

"Which?"

"Staying."

I felt heat rise in my face.

"You don't have to be so pleased with yourself."

"Impossible."

He reached for my hand across the table.

"Do you want company because you're sad," he asked, "or because you want me?"

I looked at him.

"Both. Is that allowed?"

He smiled, but there was no triumph in it.

"Of course."

I went around the table and sat beside him. He kissed me softly, then paused when I caught his collar and drew him closer. The room was warm from the little fire. Outside, the sea moved in steady breaths along the stones.

We talked for another hour, about the old notebook and the strange relief of leaving something unfinished. We laughed about his carved fish, which had a suspicious resemblance to Fen.

When I told him I wanted to go upstairs, he asked once more whether I was sure.

"I am."

We left the notebook on the table and closed the bedroom door. The rest of the night belonged to us, with no demand to make grief beautiful.

In the morning, the notebook was still there beside the little wooden fish.

I opened to the page I'd written.

Under the list, Maui had added a sentence in enormous handwriting.

YOU CAN ASK ME AGAIN TOMORROW.

I laughed so hard I nearly spilled my tea.

Then I wrote beneath it, in much smaller letters:

I probably will.
